rounds.proof_sketch: Grid launch: dim3 grid(..., N) where N=16. Thus blockIdx.z ∈ {0,1,...,15}. Original guard: bz >= 16 → FALSE for all bz ∈ {0..15}. Mutated guard: bz > 16 → FALSE for all bz ∈ {0..15}. Both predicates are unreachable since max(bz) = N-1 = 15 < N = 16.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the boundary guard from `bz >= N` to `bz > N`. With the fixed input shape (N=16 batch size), the kernel is launched with `dim3 grid(..., N)`, meaning blockIdx.z ranges from 0 to N-1 (i.e., 0 to 15). The original condition `bz >= 16` is never true since max(bz)=15. The mutated condition `bz > 16` is also never true since max(bz)=15. Both guards are unreachable dead code under this launch configuration. The mutation only affects behavior when bz=N (i.e., bz=16), but this value is impossible given grid.z=N.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation affects a boundary guard that compares blockIdx.z to N, but the grid is launched with exactly N blocks in the z-dimension, so blockIdx.z is always strictly less than N. No value-level input variation can cause blockIdx.z to reach or exceed N.
rounds.recommendations: This mutation pattern (bz >= N → bz > N) could only be killed by changing the grid launch configuration or the batch size. For kernel robustness testing, consider either: (1) marking such boundary guard mutations as configuration-dependent and requiring shape-variant tests, or (2) auditing why the guard exists (it's defensive coding for if grid.z > N) and accepting that it's dead code under the fixed N-block launch pattern.
